overview: The file consists of U.S. Department of State “List of Papers” index sheets summarizing correspondence, telegrams, memoranda, notes, and cross-references concerning newspapers in Japan from 1930 through 1939. Much of the material follows the destruction by fire of the Japan Advertiser on November 4, 1930, and Ambassador William Cameron Forbes’s efforts to preserve the influential English-language newspaper through American and Japanese financial assistance; later entries concern its reopening, official messages for Japanese newspapers, press surveys, controversial interviews and alleged misquotations, and Japanese interference with British newspapers in North China. A final, separately headed sheet indexes a presidential message congratulating the Jiji-Shimpo on its fiftieth anniversary.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Burning of the Japan Advertiser (nos. 31–32)
subfiles.about: An index sheet records Ambassador Forbes’s first reports and appeals following the destruction of the Japan Advertiser by fire.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reported that the Japan Advertiser’s building and property burned on November 4, 1930, leaving a total loss. He emphasized the newspaper’s international value and long record of usefulness and suggested approaching possible supporters. A second telegram, intended for Martin Egan at Morgan in New York, expressed hope that Egan could help the paper resume publication.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Initial Appeals to Refinance the Japan Advertiser (nos. 33–38)
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes November 1930 correspondence seeking loans and private backing to reconstruct the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The entries cover official sympathy for Fleisher, approaches to Arthur Woods and Martin Egan, and Forbes’s support for preserving a newspaper regarded as useful to international relations. Egan reported that the existing frozen loan could not be extended, although the parties wished to help. Forbes argued that additional backing could restore the paper and permit its later sale, while clarifying how insurance and liquidation would affect mortgage holders, unsecured creditors, employees, and other claimants.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Rehabilitation Plans for the Japan Advertiser (nos. 39–45)
subfiles.about: This sheet summarizes late-1930 and early-1931 negotiations over a structured American-Japanese rescue of the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Martin Egan declined the requested assistance, after which Forbes consulted Inoue about obtaining Japanese aid if American capital and a constructive business program could be secured. Forbes proposed an advisory committee and approached Geary, Place, Devault, Charles Crane, Thomas Lamont, and other New York figures. The indexed rehabilitation plan addressed the newspaper’s finances, international usefulness, managerial supervision, and rapid resumption of publication. William Stix Wasserman separately proposed that Fleisher remain editor while Merritt Hubbard take charge of business and finance.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Reopening of the Japan Advertiser and Japanese Press Matters (nos. 47–54)
subfiles.about: The sheet combines final fundraising and reopening correspondence concerning the Japan Advertiser with notes and requests involving other Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Forbes warned that time was running against the Japan Advertiser project, while Wasserman reported on fundraising discussions that included John D. Rockefeller III. Further entries proposed a finance committee and record the official congratulatory message issued when the newspaper reopened on March 26, 1931. Cross-references note hostility toward the Advertiser and a more moderate attitude toward American Far Eastern policy in the Jiji Shimpo, Hochi Shimbun, and Japan Times and Mail. The sheet also records Hornbeck’s advice against obtaining a presidential message and Kiyoshi Iwamoto’s unsuccessful request for an Acting Secretary of State message for the Hochi Shimbun’s New Year issue.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Press Surveys, Controversies, and North China Newspapers (nos. 55–65)
subfiles.about: This sheet indexes press surveys and diplomatic reporting on Japanese newspaper controversies and interference with British publications in North China through February 1939.
subfiles.summary: The early entries point to news surveys from Nagoya and Japan and to a proposed Japanese-controlled English-language newspaper for Tianjin. Grew reported that the Osaka Mainichi had attributed potentially unneutral remarks to a lieutenant colonel named Crane and that the attribution was erroneous. Another cross-reference concerns difficulties and threats arising from the Japan Advertiser’s interview with General Araki, reported by Frank Hedges. A sequence of despatches from September 1938 to February 1939 transmitted British diplomatic protests and Japanese replies concerning interference with British newspapers in North China.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Jiji-Shimpo Fiftieth-Anniversary Message
subfiles.about: A separate index sheet records the drafting, presidential approval, and transmission of a congratulatory message for the Jiji-Shimpo’s fiftieth anniversary.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes a February 25 draft telegram congratulating the Jiji-Shimpo on fifty years of service. Its wording was deliberately framed to avoid creating a troublesome precedent, and the President approved the draft. A second entry records transmission to Japan of the message signed by the President, while the sheet also supplies related decimal-file references, including one under Herbert Hoover’s name.

interest: The index sheets reveal how strongly senior American diplomats regarded an English-language newspaper as an instrument of international relations and how directly they participated in its private refinancing, including appeals to bankers, philanthropists, Japanese officials, and prospective managers. They also trace a shift from rescuing the Japan Advertiser after its 1930 fire to monitoring press attitudes, misquotation disputes, threats to correspondents, and wartime controls over foreign newspapers in North China. Although the underlying telegrams and enclosures are absent, the sheets are valuable as a roadmap to related decimal files and as evidence of the State Department’s close attention to press influence, neutrality, censorship, and ceremonial messaging.
